---
title: "Readings — End chemistry"
---

Reading is optional, but each item is here for a reason. Start with the two marked **start here**.

## Papers

**Lehman IR (1974).** *DNA ligase: structure, mechanism, and function.* Science 186:790–797.
[doi:10.1126/science.186.4166.790](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.186.4166.790)

> Why ligation needs a 5'-phosphate and a 3'-OH, in its original mechanistic form. Keep the
> adenylation steps in mind for the pre-adenylated adapters.

**Clark JM (1988).** *Novel non-templated nucleotide addition reactions catalyzed by procaryotic and eucaryotic DNA polymerases.* Nucleic Acids Research 16:9677–9686.
[doi:10.1093/nar/16.20.9677](https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/16.20.9677)

> The origin of the A-tail. Look at which polymerases do it and which base they add.

**Meissner A, et al. (2008).** *Genome-scale DNA methylation maps of pluripotent and differentiated cells.* Nature 454:766–770.
[doi:10.1038/nature07107](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature07107)

> RRBS in human and mouse cells: restriction ends, fill-in and methylated adapters in one
> method. Read the methods to see why each end step is there.

**Gu H, et al. (2011).** *Preparation of reduced representation bisulfite sequencing libraries for genome-scale DNA methylation profiling.* Nature Protocols 6:468–481.
[doi:10.1038/nprot.2010.190](https://doi.org/10.1038/nprot.2010.190) — **start here**

> The protocol version. The end repair, A-tailing and adapter steps are spelt out, with
> reasoning for each.

**Bitinaite J, et al. (2007).** *USER friendly DNA engineering and cloning method by uracil excision.* Nucleic Acids Research 35:1992–2002.
[doi:10.1093/nar/gkm041](https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkm041)

> The uracil excision reaction, as a cloning tool. The same chemistry opens hairpin adapters
> in library preparation.

**Gansauge M-T, Meyer M (2013).** *Single-stranded DNA library preparation for the sequencing of ancient or damaged DNA.* Nature Protocols 8:737–748.
[doi:10.1038/nprot.2013.038](https://doi.org/10.1038/nprot.2013.038) — **start here**

> A library with no duplex ends needed. Compare each step with a standard ligation library.

**Picelli S, et al. (2014).** *Tn5 transposase and tagmentation procedures for massively scaled sequencing projects.* Genome Research 24:2033–2040.
[doi:10.1101/gr.177881.114](https://doi.org/10.1101/gr.177881.114)

> The gap left by tagmentation and how it is filled.

**Luo C, et al. (2018).** *Robust single-cell DNA methylome profiling with snmC-seq2.* Nature Communications 9.
[doi:10.1038/s41467-018-06355-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-018-06355-2)

> Adaptase and random priming on bisulfite-converted human brain nuclei, so the end chemistry
> of single-strand tagging is seen in a human application.

## Reference material to keep open

- [NEB selection charts](https://www.neb.com/en/tools-and-resources/selection-charts) for polymerases, ligases, kinases and phosphatases.
- [NGS 101](https://henriksson-lab.github.io/NGS_101/) shows the end state at each step of every protocol.
